title: Wendell and the Aftermath
premise: Mara Kavanagh has spent nine years sending postcards to her family's burned-out house in Kilbride, writing to a mother and brother who died in the fire she may have caused. At the funeral of the town's old solicitor, a stranger named Wendell Osei greets her family by their true, abandoned surname — Delacroix — and reveals he holds letters her mother wrote before the fire, letters that name who really set it. As Mara investigates outside any courtroom, she uncovers how the town's most powerful man bought silence from police and clergy alike. The novel ends at the house sale closing: Mara reads her mother's last letter aloud on the scorched doorstep, says goodbye by name, signs the papers, and lets Wendell drive her away from Kilbride for good.
about_author: A. M. Dunmore is the pen name of a former court stenographer who spent two decades transcribing small-town trials before turning to fiction. They live near the coast and write about the sentences people never finish saying.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. We meet Mara at the post office, mailing her weekly postcard to a house that no longer exists, then deflecting a neighbor's sympathy with her practiced smile. Establishes her ritualized grief and isolation. Emotional beat: controlled numbness cracking slightly when the clerk mentions the house sale is finally scheduled.

chapters.title: A Funeral in Good Weather
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She attends solicitor Desmond Faye's funeral mostly out of obligation. A tall stranger, Wendell Osei, watches her across the graveside and later addresses her as 'Miss Delacroix' — a name unused since before the fire. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past suddenly has a witness.

chapters.title: What Wendell Carries
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. In his rented room, Wendell reviews a bundle of letters entrusted to him by Mara's dying mother years ago in another city, with instructions to deliver them only when 'the last keeper of the lie' was buried. Emotional beat: reluctant duty; he almost leaves town tonight but doesn't.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Wendell corners Mara after the reception and shows her one letter — her mother's handwriting, dated three days before the fire, mentioning 'what Thomas Rourke made us promise.' Mara refuses it and walks out. Emotional beat: terror disguised as anger.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, intercut with flashbacks. Mara visits the burned lot, now fenced for sale, and remembers the night of the fire — her argument with her brother, the smell of paraffin, her nine-year-old certainty that she was responsible. Emotional beat: guilt reasserting itself over buried memory.

chapters.title: Thomas Rourke's Good Name
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, following Mara through town. Rourke — now a county councillor and hotel owner — sponsors the memorial garden where Faye's funeral flowers were sent. Everyone speaks of him warmly; everyone also goes quiet when Mara asks about 1998. Emotional beat: the first taste of how power curates memory.

chapters.title: The Letters Wendell Won't Give Her
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Mara demands the letters; Wendell refuses, citing his promise to deliver them all at once, unopened by him. Their argument reveals his own history: a wrongful conviction he served six years for, overturned too late to matter. Emotional beat: two people recognizing each other's damage.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara visits her aunt Nuala, the only family left locally, fishing for the truth. Nuala deflects, then lets slip that Mara's father didn't abandon them — he was paid to leave and warned never to return. Emotional beat: betrayal compounding grief.

chapters.title: An Offer, Politely Made
chapters.summary: Rourke's POV. Rourke learns a stranger has been asking questions and invites Mara to his hotel, offering to buy the house sale's debts quietly and fund her 'fresh start' anywhere she likes. His charm is impeccable; his meaning unmistakable. Emotional beat: seduction and threat in the same handshake.

chapters.title: The Fire Report
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Using Faye's funeral as cover, Mara gets into his old office and finds the original fire investigation file — altered. The cause was recorded as accidental electrical fault, but a carbon copy in Faye's hand says accelerant, and names a witness who recanted. Emotional beat: cold clarity replacing self-blame.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Recanted
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell tracks down the retired guard who took the witness statement. The old man, drunk and frightened, admits he was told to lose the page — by whom he'll only write down, not say aloud. Emotional beat: the machinery of the cover-up becoming visible.

chapters.title: What Mara Was Told to Forget
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, deep flashback chapter. The full night of the fire reconstructed: her brother Eamon had witnessed Rourke's men torching a rival's property and planned to talk; her parents hid the children and went back for evidence. Mara's memory of 'causing' it was a child's story she built to survive. Emotional beat: devastating relief that curdles into rage.

chapters.title: The Postcard Returned
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. One of Mara's nine years of postcards comes back stamped 'addressee unknown' — someone at the postal depot has been reading and returning them, and included a note: 'Stop writing. He checks.' Emotional beat: surveillance dread; the past is not finished with her.

chapters.title: Nuala's Confession
chapters.summary: Nuala's POV. Nuala admits she took Rourke's money after the fire — hush money meant for the whole family — and used it to raise Mara, telling herself it was love. She begs Mara to take Rourke's offer and go. Emotional beat: shame and tenderness tangled together.

chapters.title: Burning the Offer
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara publicly declines Rourke's money at the hotel bar, quietly enough that only he hears, loudly enough that he knows witnesses exist. That night her car tires are slashed and a postcard of her own burns on her doorstep. Emotional beat: fear chosen deliberately; there is no neutral ground anymore.

chapters.title: Wendell's Decision
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell, who promised himself never to fight another town's war, finds his own conviction file referenced in Faye's papers — Rourke's influence reached into his case too. He hands Mara the full bundle of her mother's letters. Emotional beat: a man choosing to be a witness again.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Voice
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Reading the letters through the night: her mother documented everything — dates, payments, threats — and wrote a final letter addressed to Mara herself, asking forgiveness for the silence and telling her the truth was hers to spend however she needed. Emotional beat: grief transformed into inheritance.

chapters.title: The Gathering
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided. Mara, Wendell, Nuala, the retired guard, and the returned-postcard postal worker meet in Faye's empty office and assemble the record: statements, ledgers, photographs. Not for the courts, which failed them all, but for the town to read. Emotional beat: fragile solidarity; justice as testimony.

chapters.title: Publication
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The dossier appears everywhere at once — photocopied in shop windows, read aloud in the pub, sent to the county paper. Rourke's world begins shedding him; allies resign, an inquiry is announced. He confronts Mara one last time and finds nothing left to buy. Emotional beat: quiet, terrifying triumph.

chapters.title: What the Law Does Next
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Investigators arrive; the retired guard gives his statement properly this time; Rourke is charged. But Wendell reflects that the law is only catching up to what the town already decided around kitchen tables. Emotional beat: sober satisfaction — outside justice did the work, the law takes the credit.

chapters.title: Goodbye, Out Loud
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. On the morning of the closing, Mara stands on the scorched doorstep of the house and reads her mother's final letter aloud, then her own reply — forgiving her mother, forgiving her younger self, naming Eamon and her parents fully for the first time in nine years. Wendell and Nuala stand witness. Emotional beat: catharsis; the ritual completed at last.

chapters.title: The Road Out of Kilbride
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, brief coda. Papers signed, keys handed over, Mara mails one last postcard — addressed to herself, care of a new address — and gets into Wendell's car. The smile she practices in the wing mirror is, for once, real. Emotional beat: open-ended peace; memory carried rather than buried.
